summary: This informational memo describes scenarios for deploying IPv6 inside enterprise networks. It defines a small set of basic scenarios and includes questions to help administrators choose among them. It also discusses what enterprises require from IPv6 deployment.

plainLanguage.summary: A big company wants to start using the new addressing system. This document gives it a few typical plans and questions to decide which fits best.

subtitle: Reference scenarios for rolling out IPv6 in corporate networks

tldr.problem: Large organizations need clear guidance on how to transition existing IPv4 networks to IPv6, but one-size-fits-all approaches do not work because each company has different constraints and requirements.
tldr.mechanism: This document defines three base scenarios (dual-stack, sparse IPv6 for specific applications, and IPv6-dominant) and identifies critical network infrastructure components that each enterprise must analyze for their specific situation.
tldr.outcome: Enterprises can use these scenarios as templates to plan their own IPv6 rollout strategy, analyzing DNS, routing, security, applications, and management infrastructure impacts.

today: RFC 4057 is Informational and remains relevant as a planning reference for enterprises designing IPv6 strategies. It has not been obsoleted and serves as foundational guidance, though detailed transition mechanisms are covered in other RFCs referenced by this document.

sections.title: Planning IPv6 for Large Organizations
sections.content:
Enterprises deploying IPv6 face complex tradeoffs: they need to protect existing IPv4 infrastructure, support legacy applications, and integrate new IPv6 capabilities. Rather than prescribe a single strategy, this document provides three base scenarios that match common business requirements.

The audience is the enterprise network team tasked with designing IPv6 deployment. That usually includes management, operations, and engineering staff. Each organization will select the transition approach that best supports its business goals, which is why the document provides abstract templates rather than concrete steps.
sections.plainLanguage: Different companies need different plans based on what they use their network for. This document gives three general types of plans to choose from.

sections.title: The Three Base Scenarios
sections.content:
The first scenario assumes the enterprise decides to deploy IPv6 in conjunction with existing IPv4, running both protocols in parallel on most of the network (called dual-stack). The enterprise keeps its IPv4 investments protected and functional while gradually moving workloads to IPv6.

The second scenario is sparse IPv6 deployment, where the enterprise runs IPv6 only for a specific set of applications that require it, leaving the bulk of the network on IPv4. This minimizes disruption but limits IPv6 benefits to particular use cases.

The third scenario is IPv6-dominant, where a company building a new network or restructuring an existing one makes IPv6 the primary protocol, with IPv4 coexisting for legacy systems. This approach works best for companies willing to redesign their infrastructure from scratch.
sections.plainLanguage: Scenario one: run both IPv4 and IPv6 everywhere. Scenario two: use IPv6 only for certain apps. Scenario three: make IPv6 the main system and keep IPv4 for old things.

sections.title: Infrastructure Components to Analyze
sections.content:
Each scenario requires analysis of critical infrastructure: DNS must support both IPv4 and IPv6 records; routing protocols must handle both stacks and transition mechanisms; host configuration must choose between stateless and stateful autoconfiguration. Enterprises must also plan address space allocation, considering both the IPv4 addresses they currently own and the IPv6 space assigned by providers.

Security policies, firewall rules, and access controls must be redesigned to work with IPv6. Load balancers, network management systems, and intrusion detection tools often lack IPv6 support and may require replacement or workarounds. The organization must also verify that applications and devices—from servers to printers—can handle IPv6 addresses and traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: The company must check that DNS, routers, firewalls, servers, and printers all understand IPv6. If some do not, it needs a workaround or upgrade plan.

sections.title: Real-World Deployment Examples
sections.content:
Example Network A is a distributed enterprise across multiple geographically separated sites connected by leased lines. External connectivity exists but the provider does not offer IPv6 service. The enterprise runs internal mail, file servers, and Java applications, with network management via SNMP. Some hardware (like load balancers) does not support IPv6, creating gaps in the deployment.

Example Network B is a bank with a multi-site private network using VPN connections and supporting mobile workforce access from outside. Transaction processing is critical and geographically distributed. Network mobility and address management become complex when IPv6 is introduced.

Example Network C is a mission-critical network like a defense or emergency operation center where every node may move, encryption is mandatory, and high availability is non-negotiable. The network must absorb on-the-fly sub-networks and configure nodes without a central server, pushing IPv6 to its limits and requiring the most sophisticated deployment approach.
sections.plainLanguage: A company with many office buildings connected by private lines faces different challenges than a bank with mobile remote workers or a military command center with moving units.

sections.title: Security and Next Steps
sections.content:
The RFC does not detail security issues in IPv6 deployment itself, but notes that each scenario will have distinct security challenges that must be addressed when analyzing that scenario. Firewalls and intrusion detection systems must be evaluated and potentially upgraded to understand IPv6 headers and traffic patterns.

The document ends by noting that a detailed analysis of tools and mechanisms to support the scenarios will be published separately. Enterprises should use these base scenarios and infrastructure components as a checklist to define their specific requirements, rather than adopting one scenario unchanged.
sections.plainLanguage: Security issues are important but depend on which scenario a company picks. The document says the detailed how-to guide will come later.
